blocks.text: In the 21st century, the word "hazolonialism" still continues to be used as a rhetorical weapon. Every Western intervention is immediately suspected of being a new dominance effort. That's the charge that is now directed at Trump Gaza Plan, an idea of reconstruction Gaza in post-war with a model of the technology transition government, led by international figures. Critics call it the face of 21st century colonialism: puppet government, economic exploitation, and threat of violence.
But is the accusation accurate? Or, more importantly, does he just extend the suffering of the Palestinian people by allowing violent ideology to remain uninterrupted in Gaza?

Classic colonialism history, either by VOC or European imperium, is clearly directed at a permanent accumulation of wealth. Colonies never depart from the intent of building, but to exploit. Gaza is different today. There's no spice or gold that makes it globally attractive. Gaza is not a resource, it's an ideology that, more accurately, Hamas' ideology that rejects the existence of Jews and makes permanent violence a raison d Ezatre.

To quote Frantz Fanon or Edward Said to attack Trump just missed the target. Fanon's talking about the emancipatorial resistance to colonialism. But Hamas' violence is not an empathic resistance; it's ideological violence that rejects peace. Said criticizing Western construction which weakened the East, but Hamas himself kept Gaza's image as a land of chaos in order to gain international sympathy.
Stille Mbembe writes about necropolitical life-death politics. But who better to run this logic than Hamas who makes his people shield alive?

Trump Gaza Plan is tough. He demanded de- militarization quickly, and yes, there was a nuance of coercion. But in the political world of realists, security has always been a prerequisition of development. Gaza cannot move towards well-being during Hamas to make war an identity. The tecnocratic transition Trump proposed was not permanent colonialism, but the post-ideology politics opened up the space so people could get Gaza out of the grip of armed groups.

Those who reject this plan under the pretext of an anticolonial actually offer what? Status quo? The status quo means Gaza remains controlled by Hamas, the people remain poor, and the war never ends. Ironically, the anticolonial rhetoric intended to defend Palestine only made Palestine continue to suffer.

Trump Gaza Plan is not a perfect solution, but he dares to touch the root of the problem: Gaza cannot be free under the ideology of hatred. The world may be cynical, but without a brave political breakthrough, the people of Gaza will live under the ruins. The question is not whether Trump's plan is colonialism, but whether the world dares to see the suffering of the Palestinian people without constantly covering it with an empty anticolonial slogan.
